title: CDNs
subtitle: Serve cacheable responses near users and control edge freshness
objectives: Explain why distance is a latency floor and what putting content at the edge buys
Decide what belongs on a CDN and what doesn't, using cacheability rather than file type
Invalidate edge caches correctly, and know why versioned URLs beat purging
Reason about hit ratio, origin shielding, and what a CDN cannot do for you

exercises.title: Network distance imposes a propagation-delay floor on latency
exercises.body: Signals propagate through optical fibre at about 200,000 km/s. A 1,000 km one-way path therefore contributes about 10 ms to a round trip before routing, queueing, protocol handshakes, or application work. Serving the response from a nearby edge reduces that path length.
exercises.note: Geographic distance is a latency lower bound. Real Internet routes are longer than straight-line distance and add router and exchange-point delay.

exercises.prompt: A product launch sends 50,000 static-image requests per second to an origin that handles 1,000. Cache 99% of image requests at CDN edges.
exercises.result: The edge absorbed 49,500 requests each second
exercises.why: A 99% CDN hit rate leaves 1% of 50,000 requests, or 500 req/s, for the origin. A cache miss still reaches the origin, so launch readiness depends on both hit rate and origin capacity.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: A product launch sends 50,000 static-image requests per second to an origin that handles 1,000. Cache 99% of image requests at CDN edges. Place CDN edge, Origin. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Global users → CDN edge; CDN edge → Origin. That topology is the evidence for the answer: A 99% CDN hit rate leaves 1% of 50,000 requests, or 500 req/s, for the origin. A cache miss still reaches the origin, so launch readiness depends on both hit rate and origin capacity.

exercises.prompt: Your servers are in Virginia. A user in Sydney loads your site. Your server responds in 5ms. Why does the page still feel slow?
choices: The request has to cross the planet and back — physics puts a floor under that round trip that no server speed can fix
exercises.why: The request and response must traverse long network paths between Sydney and Virginia. Propagation and routing impose a round-trip latency far larger than the server's 5ms processing time, so optimizing the server cannot remove the distance-dependent floor.

exercises.prompt: A ______ is a network of servers spread around the world that keep copies of your content close to users.
exercises.why: A content delivery network (CDN) caches content on geographically distributed edge servers. When a nearby edge has a fresh cached object, it answers the request locally, reducing network distance, origin traffic, and response latency.

exercises.prompt: So what does a CDN actually do about the Sydney problem?
choices: It makes your Virginia server faster
On a cache hit, a Sydney edge returns its local copy without an origin round trip across the ocean
It compresses the response so it travels faster
exercises.why: A Sydney edge can return its cached copy locally, removing the Virginia round trip from a cache hit. The edge copy is derived from the origin, so its freshness is controlled by cache policy and invalidation.

exercises.prompt: A Sydney edge misses on `/logo.svg`. Complete the fetch path so this request reaches the authority and the next nearby request can hit a copy.
exercises.why: The nearby edge checks its cache first; on this miss it fetches the authoritative object from the origin, returns it, and stores a copy under the response's cache policy. If the origin is unavailable during the miss and no permitted stale copy exists, this request fails even though later edge hits would not need the origin.

exercises.prompt: Match each CDN term to what it means.

pairs.right: Your actual server, the source of truth
The edge had to ask the origin

exercises.why: An edge or point of presence (PoP) is a nearby CDN location, while the origin is the authoritative server. A hit is served from the edge copy; a miss requires an origin fetch and can populate that copy for subsequent requests.

exercises.prompt: Besides latency, what does serving from the edge also reduce?
choices: Load on your origin — requests served at the edge never reach your servers at all
exercises.why: A cache hit terminates at the edge, so it consumes no origin request capacity or origin egress for that response. When shared assets dominate traffic, a high edge hit ratio can remove most of that workload from the origin.

exercises.title: An edge response is cacheable when requests can reuse one fresh representation
exercises.body: A content delivery network (CDN) stores an origin response under a cache key at an edge. Later requests reuse it only when they produce the same key and the stored response is still fresh. Shared assets and public pages usually provide reuse; personalized responses usually do not.
exercises.note: A cache key that mixes users incorrectly can expose private data. A key fragmented by unnecessary variants sends most requests back to the origin.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: An edge response is cacheable when requests can reuse one fresh representation
exercises.why: A content delivery network (CDN) stores an origin response under a cache key at an edge. Later requests reuse it only when they produce the same key and the stored response is still fresh. Shared assets and public pages usually provide reuse; personalized responses usually do not. A cache key that mixes users incorrectly can expose private data. A key fragmented by unnecessary variants sends most requests back to the origin.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is the easiest thing to serve from a CDN?
choices: Your logo image — identical for every user, changes almost never
exercises.why: The logo has identical bytes for every requester, changes rarely, and tolerates a stale copy, so one edge object can serve many users. Personalized dashboards and balances require per-user isolation, while live chat requires tighter freshness than this shared cache policy provides.

exercises.prompt: What actually decides whether something can be cached at the edge?
choices: Whether it's an image or a script
Whether many people ask for the identical thing, and whether being slightly out of date is acceptable
exercises.why: Edge caching is effective when many requests use the same cache key and response bytes, and when the response may remain stale for the configured interval. File type alone does not establish either property: shared HTML can cache safely, while personalized media may not.

exercises.prompt: Which of these can usually be served from a CDN? Select all.
choices: A page showing the logged-in user's name
exercises.why: The JavaScript bundle, product image, and public post can use shared cache entries because their responses are identical across users. A logged-in page varies by identity; caching it without a correctly partitioned private key can serve one user's content to another.

exercises.prompt: How does the edge know how long it may keep a copy?
choices: Your origin tells it, using cache headers like `Cache-Control` with a max-age
It always keeps things for 24 hours
exercises.why: The origin's `Cache-Control` directives tell shared caches whether a response may be stored and how long it remains fresh. A `max-age` value defines the freshness interval, after which the edge must revalidate, refetch, or apply another permitted stale-response policy.

exercises.prompt: You set max-age to 1 year on a file you might need to change. Reckless?
choices: Yes — you can never update it
No, provided the filename changes whenever the content does: `app.a3f9c1.js` is cached forever precisely because a new build produces a new name
Yes — a year is always too long
No, because you can always purge
exercises.why: A content hash in the filename changes whenever the bytes change. The URL therefore identifies immutable content, allowing a one-year freshness period; a new build publishes a new URL that has no stale cached representation.

exercises.prompt: Why is the `index.html` that references those hashed files usually cached for a very short time — or not at all?
choices: HTML is too big to cache
Because it's the one file whose name never changes, so it's the only place that can tell browsers which new hashed files to fetch
HTML can't be cached by CDNs
exercises.why: `index.html` is a stable URL that points to the current content-hashed assets. If that pointer remains cached for a long time, clients continue requesting old asset names after deployment, so the pointer needs a short freshness interval even though the hashed assets can be cached for a year.

exercises.title: Freshness metadata controls when an edge contacts the origin again
exercises.body: `Cache-Control: max-age=86400` marks a response fresh for 86,400 seconds. During that interval, an edge may serve its stored bytes without contacting the origin. Updating the origin does not notify those copies; they change after expiry, revalidation, purge, or a request for a new URL.
exercises.note: A long freshness lifetime can keep an incorrect response active at many edges. Use versioned URLs for immutable assets or retain a reliable purge path for stable URLs.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: Freshness metadata controls when an edge contacts the origin again
exercises.why: `Cache-Control: max-age=86400` marks a response fresh for 86,400 seconds. During that interval, an edge may serve its stored bytes without contacting the origin. Updating the origin does not notify those copies; they change after expiry, revalidation, purge, or a request for a new URL. A long freshness lifetime can keep an incorrect response active at many edges. Use versioned URLs for immutable assets or retain a reliable purge path for stable URLs.

exercises.prompt: You publish a typo, then fix it. But the wrong version is cached at 300 edge locations with a 24-hour max-age. What's the problem?
choices: Your fix is live at the origin, but users keep getting the typo from the edge until those copies expire
The edges will notice the change automatically
Only Sydney users see the typo
exercises.why: Each edge considers its cached object fresh for the configured 24-hour interval and does not check the origin during that period. Updating the origin alone leaves those copies eligible, so users continue receiving the typo until expiry or explicit invalidation.

exercises.prompt: Match each way of dealing with stale edge copies.

pairs.right: Wait it out — the copy dies on schedule
Tell the CDN to drop it now
Change the name so nothing is stale
Edge asks the origin: still current?

exercises.why: Time-to-live expiry waits for the freshness interval, purge actively removes cached objects, a versioned URL creates a new cache key, and revalidation asks the origin whether the existing object is current. Each mechanism trades origin work, operational action, and update latency differently.

exercises.prompt: Why do versioned URLs beat purging as a default strategy?
choices: A content-derived filename gives new bytes a new cache key, so an old object cannot answer a request for that new asset version
exercises.why: When immutable asset bytes change, a content-derived filename changes the cache key, so an old object cannot answer a request for the new asset URL. Purging requires a separate invalidation operation that can be missed or delayed. Clients with stale HTML may still request the old version, so the HTML pointer needs its own freshness policy.

exercises.prompt: When is purging genuinely the right tool?
choices: When the URL must stay the same and the content changed — a published article being corrected, say
exercises.why: A published article must preserve its stable bookmarked and indexed URL, so changing the cache key would change the public resource address. Purging invalidates the existing edge copies while keeping that URL intact, allowing the corrected origin response to repopulate them.

exercises.prompt: Your CDN supports '`stale-while-revalidate`': serve the cached copy immediately, and refresh it in the background. What are you buying?
choices: Speed for the user right now, at the cost of that one response being slightly out of date
exercises.why: `stale-while-revalidate` permits the edge to return an expired copy immediately while one background request refreshes it. The current requester avoids origin latency, while accepting that response's bounded staleness until the refreshed object replaces it.

exercises.prompt: A news homepage may be at most 60 seconds stale. With a 60-second `TTL` and 240 active edge locations, about how many origin refreshes per second occur if each edge refreshes once per `TTL`?
exercises.why: The freshness target caps the time to live at 60 seconds. At that value, 240 edge locations ÷ 60 seconds = about 4 origin refreshes per second, collapsing enormous viewer traffic into a small origin load; `stale-while-revalidate` can serve the old object while each refresh completes.

exercises.title: A CDN hit requires an exact cache-key match and a reusable response
exercises.body: An edge derives a cache key from the request URL and any request headers named by `Vary`. It serves a hit only when an unexpired stored response has the identical key and its cache policy permits reuse. Otherwise, the edge forwards the request toward the origin.
exercises.note: Unique query parameters and broad `Vary` rules fragment one object into many keys. Each variant must be fetched and warmed separately, increasing origin traffic.

exercises.prompt: Your CDN reports a 60% cache hit ratio. Is that good?
choices: It depends what's in the other 40%, but for static assets it's poor: 40% of requests are still crossing to your origin
exercises.why: A 60% hit ratio leaves 40% of requests reaching the origin. For immutable shared assets, repeated requests should normally reuse edge objects, so this ratio warrants checking cache keys, freshness headers, and response variation; the acceptable ratio still depends on which objects make up the misses.

exercises.prompt: A popular file expires at 300 edge locations at the same moment, and traffic is heavy. What happens to your origin?
choices: Up to 300 simultaneous fetches for the same file hit your origin at once — a thundering herd
exercises.why: Each of the 300 edges can observe expiry and initiate its own origin fetch, producing up to 300 concurrent requests for one file. Per-edge request coalescing limits each location to one fetch, while an origin shield can further combine those edge misses before they reach the origin.

exercises.prompt: Build an origin-shield path. Many regional edge misses should converge on one cache layer before any request reaches the origin.
exercises.why: Regional edges use the origin shield as their upstream cache, so concurrent misses for one object can collapse into one fetch before reaching the origin. If the shield is unavailable and no bypass path exists, it becomes a choke point for misses; even when healthy, a shield miss adds another hop before the origin responds.

exercises.prompt: Which of these quietly destroy your cache hit ratio? Select all.
choices: Appending a unique tracking parameter like ?t=1234 to asset URLs
A `Vary` header that splits one file into many per-browser variants
Returning `Cache-Control: private, no-store` for a shared asset
Serving the same file to every user
exercises.why: A unique query parameter creates a distinct cache key for each request, an over-broad `Vary` header partitions one response into many variants, and `private, no-store` explicitly forbids shared storage. Missing cache directives are not an unambiguous cache killer because CDN rules or heuristic caching may still store some responses.

exercises.prompt: Your API returns different private data for each user and each user rarely repeats the same request. Will shared CDN caching fix the slow backend work?
choices: Usually no — cross-user reuse is unsafe, and rare repeat requests give a private per-user cache little reuse
exercises.why: A shared cache must never reuse one user's private response for another user. Identity-aware cache keys can permit private reuse for repeated requests from the same user; the prompt states that such reuse is rare. A CDN can still accelerate connection setup and transport, while the slow application work remains at the origin.

exercises.prompt: You deploy a fix. Some users see it, some still see the bug, and refreshing sometimes helps. What's the most likely explanation?
choices: Different caches are at different stages — some edges hold the old copy, and some browsers hold their own copy too
The users are on old devices
exercises.why: Browsers, intermediary caches, CDN edges, and shields can each hold an independently fresh copy. Requests routed through different cache paths therefore see different versions until those entries expire, revalidate, or are invalidated; a versioned URL bypasses all old keys.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of a CDN?
choices: It makes your whole site faster automatically
It's a cache near your users: it shortens distance and absorbs origin load for content many people share — and it hands you invalidation across machines you don't control
exercises.why: A CDN serves reusable content from nearby edge copies, reducing propagation latency and origin load. Because those copies are distributed and may remain fresh after the origin changes, the design must specify cache keys, freshness intervals, invalidation, and acceptable staleness.

exercises.prompt: A CDN caches `/dashboard` without varying by identity. One user's account summary is served to another user. What design rule was violated?
choices: Private responses require no shared reuse or an identity-safe cache key
Every HTML response must be public
exercises.why: A shared cache reused a representation across identities that were not equivalent. Private data must bypass shared caching or use a key and policy that prevents cross-user reuse.
